title: kitchen.json
description: A Kitchen project's build and runtime settings, committed beside the code they describe. Read from the project's root directory at the commit under build; the settings it names win over the ones set in the dashboard, and it says nothing about the ones it does not name. It cannot carry a credential, and it cannot set the project's root directory, criticality, data class, access or preview protection.

$schema.description: This document, so an editor can complete the file. The platform reads the key only to ignore it.

strategy.description: auto reads the repository and decides — a Dockerfile wins, and everything else recognised goes to buildpacks. Naming one skips that decision.

dockerfilePath.description: Path to the Dockerfile, relative to the project's root directory, which it may not leave. Used when the strategy is, or resolves to, dockerfile.

dockerfileTarget.description: Which stage of a multi-stage Dockerfile produces the image to run. Leave it out to ship the file's last stage. A stage the file does not declare fails the build, and so does naming one on a commit built with buildpacks, which has no stages.

runtime.description: How the built image runs. Every key is optional, and one left out keeps whatever the project has.

port.description: The port the application listens on, and the value of PORT in every environment. Leave it out to take the detected framework's.

replicas.description: Copies of the application in production environments. Previews always run one.

singleton.description: Two of this workload must never run at once, so a deploy stops the old copy before starting the new one. Refuses replicas above 1.

notRequestDriven.description: This workload does work nobody asked for, so no environment of the project is ever idled to zero — previews included.

command.description: Replaces the image's entrypoint, in exec form: a list of words, never a shell line.

args.description: Replaces the image's arguments, in exec form.

previewArgs.description: Replaces args in preview environments — the same commit and artifact, different flags.

resources.description: What the workload asks for, as request and limit alike.

env.description: Environment variables, by name. Values are literal strings and nothing else: this file is committed, so everything in it is public. A variable that should come from a secret or a provisioned resource is set in the dashboard or with `kitchen env set`, and a name declared here that the project already binds to one of those fails the build rather than shadowing it.

previewEnv.description: Values that replace the ones in env for preview environments. Every name here must also be in env: a preview value replaces a value, so the variable has to have one.

processes.description: The workloads this project runs besides its web process: workers, services, scheduled jobs, and the tasks that run once per deploy before any of the release takes traffic. Declaring this replaces the project's whole list rather than merging into it — a worker the commit no longer names is one whose command may no longer be in the image.

files.description: The configuration files this commit places into its workloads. Software the platform did not build is often configured by a file at a fixed path rather than by environment variables — Home Assistant's configuration.yaml, Gitea's app.ini — and this is where one is declared. Each is mounted read-only at its path into every workload it names, and is frozen into the release, so a rollback restores the file that release ran with. Declaring one merges onto the project's list by name, unlike processes: a project may hold a secret file this file may not declare, and a list that replaced would take it away. A file is placed exactly as written — nothing is substituted into it from the environment.

configFile.description: One configuration file: what is in it, where it goes, and which of this project's workloads read it.

name.description: A name for the file, and the key every surface refers to it by — letters, digits, '-', '_' and '.'. It is not the path, so a file that moves keeps its name.

path.description: Where the file appears inside the container: absolute, and naming the file itself rather than the directory holding it. Only that one path is replaced; the rest of the directory stays the image's.

content.description: The file, verbatim. It is required here, unlike on the API, because a committed declaration has nowhere else to have put it.

workloads.description: The workloads that mount the file: "web" for the web process, and the name of any workload this file declares. Leave it out and every workload of the project gets it.

secret.description: Refused here, and described so that the refusal is findable rather than arriving as an unknown field. This file is committed, so everything in it is public, and whether the platform holds a credential for a project is not something a commit gets to declare — set a secret file in the dashboard or with `kitchen files set --secret`.

security.description: The security posture every workload of this project runs under — the web process, its workers and its scheduled runs, since they are one image. An empty object is the platform's default, which every workload gets anyway: the runtime's own seccomp profile, and no privilege escalation. Everything else here is a tightening the application asks for, because an image that writes to its own filesystem or runs as root is ordinary and the platform will not break one silently.

runAsNonRoot.description: Refuse to start a container whose image would run as uid 0. The kubelet checks it before the container starts, so the failure names the constraint instead of appearing three layers down.

runAsUser.description: The uid the containers run as, overriding the image's. 0 is the image's own user left alone, not a request to run as root.

runAsGroup.description: The gid the containers run as. 0 is the image's own, as for runAsUser.

fsGroup.description: The gid that owns the volumes mounted into the containers. A freshly provisioned volume comes up owned by root, so a workload running as anybody else is handed one it cannot write; the kubelet chowns it to this gid before the container starts. 0 is the volume's own ownership left alone.

fsGroupChangePolicy.description: When that ownership is applied. Left out it is Kubernetes' default, Always, which walks the whole volume on every start; OnRootMismatch skips the walk when the volume's own root already matches, which is what a large persistent volume wants — at the price of a subtree left behind by a previous uid staying unwritable. It needs an fsGroup to apply and is refused without one.

readOnlyRootFilesystem.description: Mount the container's own filesystem read only. An application that writes to a path it did not declare fails on the write rather than on the next node it lands on.

allowPrivilegeEscalation.description: Put back the one default the platform tightens: left alone, no process in the container can gain more privileges than its parent. Set it for an image that legitimately needs a setuid binary.

dropCapabilities.description: Linux capabilities taken away, in the kernel's spelling without the CAP_ prefix — or the single entry ALL. There is no list to add one back: the platform drops none by default.

health.description: What the platform asks the workload before it sends anyone to it. An empty object is the default: a TCP connect to the port, on the platform's timings.

path.description: The HTTP path a probe asks for; a 2xx or 3xx is the application saying it is working. Left out, the check is a TCP connect instead.

port.description: The port the probe is made against, when it is not the one the application is published on. A process publishes none, so a process's check must name one.

periodSeconds.description: How often the check is made. Default 10.

timeoutSeconds.description: How long one check may take. Default 2.

failureThreshold.description: How many failures in a row take a running container out of service. Default 3.

startupFailureThreshold.description: How many the same check may fail while the container is still starting. Default 30.

name.description: A DNS label, and not "web": the web process is the project's own runtime, and this list is what it runs besides it.

type.description: A worker runs continuously and is never addressed; a cron process runs on a schedule; a service runs continuously and is addressed by the rest of the unit over the cluster network, and is never published; a task runs once per deploy and has to finish before any of that release takes traffic, which is where a schema migration goes. A task that fails stops the deploy where it stands, and whatever was serving keeps serving.

command.description: Exec form: a list of words.

args.description: Exec form: a list of words, appended to the command.

port.description: The port a service listens on, and the port its siblings reach it on. Required on a service and refused on anything else: only a service is addressed.

replicas.description: A worker's copy count. Zero is a worker that is declared and parked.

singleton.description: Two of this workload must never run at once, so a deploy stops the old copy before starting the new one. Refuses replicas above 1, and refused on a scheduled process — whether two of its runs may overlap is concurrencyPolicy — and on a task, which is one run per deploy and has no second copy to overlap.

schedule.description: A cron process's five-field expression, read in UTC. Required for type cron and refused on every other type — a worker and a service run continuously, and a task runs once per deploy.

concurrencyPolicy.description: What a scheduled process does when a run is due and the last one has not finished. Default Forbid.

timeout.description: A Go duration bounding one run — a scheduled one, or a task's, which is how long the deploy waits for it before calling it failed. Default an hour.

previews.description: Run this workload in preview environments too. A worker and a scheduled job are off unless asked for; a service and a task are on unless they say otherwise, because a preview missing one of its own services — or with a database branch nothing migrated — is a broken preview.

imageSource.description: An image this platform did not build, and the third answer to the question build asks: a repository somebody else publishes and a tag or a digest of it. It excludes build — a workload is built here or published elsewhere, never both — and a unit may mix the two, shipping an upstream image beside a sidecar built from this repository in one release.

repository.description: Where the image lives, registry host included and without a tag or a digest.

tag.description: The version as the vendor publishes it. A tag or a digest is required; naming both means this tag, and it must still be this content.

digest.description: The exact content. It is what the release records whichever of the two is declared, because a tag is a moving target and a rollback that followed one would not be a rollback.

connection.description: The Connection this image is pulled with, holding a docker config for its registry. Leave it out for a public image, which is pulled anonymously. It is never the connection the project pushes its own builds to.

processBuild.description: This workload's own build, for a repository that ships several images from one commit. Absent means it runs the project's image with another command, which is one build rather than two. Refused on a scheduled process.

strategy.description: How the image is produced. Default auto, which reads this workload's own rootDirectory and decides: a Dockerfile there wins, otherwise the framework detected there is built with buildpacks, otherwise the build fails naming this workload.

dockerfilePath.description: The Dockerfile, relative to rootDirectory. Default Dockerfile.

dockerfileTarget.description: Which stage of this workload's multi-stage Dockerfile produces its image. Leave it out to build the stage the project names — its build.dockerfileTarget, or the file's last stage where the project names none either. A stage the file does not declare fails the build naming this workload, and so does naming one on a workload built with buildpacks, which has no stages.

rootDirectory.description: The directory of the repository this workload is built from, relative to the repository root — not to the project's own root directory.
